title: Tazria: pray for the one outside (Leviticus 13:45–46)
hookLine: the afflicted cries "unclean"; the Talmud says so that others will pray for him (Shabbat 67a)

cards: It's one of the loneliest pictures in the Torah. Someone declared to have tzara'at tears their clothes, leaves their hair loose, covers their lip: the signs of a mourner. They live alone, outside the camp.
And when anyone approaches, they have to call out a word. Read plainly, it sounds like a warning label: stay back. That's how many readers have heard it.
The Talmud hears something else in the same cry.

teach.b: The verses, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: the person shall cry, "Unclean, unclean." And: "he shall dwell alone; without the camp shall his dwelling be."
In tractate Shabbat, the rabbis ask why he has to announce it at all.
Their answer: so that he makes his pain known to many, and many will ask for mercy for him. The cry isn't only keep away. It's also: I'm here, I'm suffering, remember me.
The person outside can't come in. But the people inside can still pray, if they pray, and they can remember. The boundary stays, and the bond stays too.

teach.h: THE MI SHEBERAKH FOR THE SICK.
teach.b: Jewish practice carries this forward in a prayer called the mi sheberakh for the sick, said at the Torah reading, where the names of people who are ill are spoken aloud so the whole congregation holds them.
Some people ask to have their own name read. In this tradition, telling others isn't weakness. It's how you let them carry you a little.

teach.h: A WEEK OF GRIEF AND SKIN.
teach.b: And the cry closes a hard week. Aaron's sons died and Aaron grieved, first in silence, then with reasons Moses accepted. Shemini ended with kadosh, holy in the everyday.
Tazria began with a birth, then tzara'at, a priest who must look, and a priest who waits.
Now a person outside the camp, whose cry asks the camp to pray.

how: In many synagogues, during the Torah reading, the congregation says the mi sheberakh prayer for the sick, naming people who are ill, often with their Hebrew name and their mother's name.

games.q: you're outside the camp with tzara'at, and someone is walking toward you. what does the Torah have you do?
games.why: you cry out. and the Talmud says the point is not only warning: it's so that many will hear and pray for you.

practice: Think of someone who is outside the camp right now: sick at home, in a hospital, grieving alone, far away, or just lonely in a full house. Say their name to yourself.
If you pray, ask for mercy for them in your own words or with a prayer you know; if you don't, simply hold them in mind with care.

wordCard.voice: Tazria. The portion that ends with a person crying out from outside the camp, so that others will pray for them.

orig.note: Hebrew: "unclean, unclean": the cry of Leviticus 13:45.

carryVoice: Your line: pray for the one outside. A cry can also be a way of asking to be held. Another week behind you.
